title_en: China Construction Bank Corporation Guangzhou Liwan Branch v. Guangdong Lanyue Energy Development Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over letter of credit issuance
ruling_gist_en: A bill of lading has the dual attributes of being an instrument of creditor's rights and an instrument of title. Whether the holder of a bill of lading acquires real rights due to receipt of delivery of the bill of lading, and what type of real rights are acquired, depends on the contract terms. In this case, the issuing bank held the bill of lading pursuant to the contract between it and the applicant. Taking into account the true intent of the parties and the characteristics of letter of credit transactions, it should be determined that the issuing bank has a pledge right over the bill of lading in the documents under the letter of credit and over the goods covered by the bill of lading. The method by which the issuing bank exercises the pledge over the bill of lading is the same as the method for exercising a pledge over movable property under the bill of lading, i.e., it has the right to be paid in priority from the proceeds obtained from discounting, selling, or auctioning the goods covered by the bill of lading.
keywords_en: Civil; Letter of credit issuance dispute; Retrial; Supreme People's Court; Guangdong Province; Legal person; Financial institution; Natural person; Contract Law; Property Law; Security Law; Nature of bill of lading as document of title; Issuing bank's pledge right over bill of lading; Legal nature of trust receipt; Amended judgment; Letter of credit issuance; Pledge of bill of lading; Trust receipt; Coal import; Good faith; Real rights; Pledge right; Limited company and other letter of credit issuance disputes
full_text_en:
China Construction Bank Corporation, Guangzhou Liwan Branch v. Guangdong Lanyue Energy Development Co., Ltd. et al. — Dispute over Letter of Credit Issuance

【Ruling Summary】

A bill of lading possesses the dual attributes of a document of obligation and a document of title. Whether the holder of a bill of lading acquires real rights by accepting delivery of the bill of lading, and the type of real rights acquired, depends on the contractual provisions. In this case, the issuing bank held the bill of lading pursuant to the contract between it and the applicant for the letter of credit. Considering the true intention of the parties and the characteristics of letter of credit transactions, it should be determined that the issuing bank holds a right of pledge over the bill of lading contained in the documents under the letter of credit and over the goods covered by the bill of lading. The method by which the issuing bank exercises the right of pledge over the bill of lading is the same as the method for exercising a pledge over movable property under the bill of lading, namely, it has the right to be paid in priority from the proceeds obtained from the discount, sale, or auction of the goods under the bill of lading.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court
(2015) Min Ti Zi No. 126

Re-applicant (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): China Construction Bank Corporation, Guangzhou Liwan Branch. Domicile: No. 304, Zhongshan Qi Lu, Liwan District, Guangzhou City, Guangdong Province.
Responsible Person: Luo Tiefeng, Branch Manager.
Agent ad litem: You Tao, Lawyer, Guangdong Qiangbang Law Firm.
Agent ad litem: Yan Liang, Lawyer, Guangdong Qiangbang Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Guangdong Lanyue Energy Development Co., Ltd. Domicile: Room C, 19/F, Yinghu Xuan, Building B, Luhu Mansion, No. 128 Lujing Road, Yuexiu District, Guangzhou City, Guangdong Province.
Representative of Litigation: Jiang Bin, Person in Charge of the Administrator of the Company.
Agent ad litem: Zhuang Qiongsen, Staff Member of the Company.
Agent ad litem: Lan Duanhua, Staff Member of the Company.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Huilai Yuedong Electric Power Fuel Co., Ltd. Domicile: No. 5 Kuihe Road, Kuitan Town, Huilai County, Jieyang City, Guangdong Province.
Legal Representative: Lan Wenbin, Chairman of the Company.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Guangdong Blue Sea Shipping Co., Ltd. Domicile: Room 19B, No. 128 Lujing Road, Yuexiu District, Guangzhou City, Guangdong Province.
Representative of Litigation: Jiang Bin, Person in Charge of the Administrator of the Company.
Agent ad litem: Zhang Guoxin, Staff Member of the Company.
Agent ad litem: Ban Riyin, Staff Member of the Company.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Lan Wenbin.
Agent ad litem: Zhuang Qiongsen.
Agent ad litem: Lan Duanhua, Daughter of Lan Wenbin.

The re-applicant, China Construction Bank Corporation, Guangzhou Liwan Branch (hereinafter referred to as CCB Liwan Branch), due to a dispute with the respondents, Guangdong Lanyue Energy Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Lanyue Energy), Huilai Yuedong Electric Power Fuel Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yuedong Electric Power), Guangdong Blue Sea Shipping Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Blue Sea Shipping), and Lan Wenbin, over letter of credit issuance, being dissatisfied with the Civil Judgment (2014) Yue Gao Fa Min Er Zhong Zi No. 45 of the Guangdong High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as Guangdong High Court), applied to this Court for retrial. This Court, on June 29, 2015, rendered the Civil Ruling (2015) Min Shen Zi No. 1461, granting retrial of this case, and, in accordance with the law, formed a collegial panel and held a public hearing of this case on July 20, 2015. The agents ad litem of CCB Liwan Branch, You Tao and Yan Liang, the common agents ad litem of Lanyue Energy and Lan Wenbin, Zhuang Qiongsen and Lan Duanhua, and the agents ad litem of Blue Sea Shipping, Zhang Guoxin and Ban Riyin, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. Yuedong Electric Power, having been summoned by subpoena from this Court, failed to appear in court without justifiable reasons, and this Court proceeded with the trial by default in accordance with the law. The trial of this case has now been concluded.

CCB Liwan Branch filed a lawsuit with the Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court of Guangdong Province (hereinafter referred to as Guangzhou Intermediate Court), requesting a judgment: 1. That Lanyue Energy repay CCB Liwan Branch the principal of the letter of credit advance payment in the amount of RMB 84,867,952.27 (unless otherwise specified, the currency below is RMB) and interest (including penalty interest and compound interest, calculated at a daily rate of 0.05%, calculated from March 8, 2013, and tentatively calculated up to March 21, 2013, as RMB 551,641.70) up to the date of full repayment; 2. That the 164,998 tons of coal under the aforesaid letter of credit be confirmed as the property of CCB Liwan Branch, and that the proceeds from the disposal of such property be used to satisfy the debts under the aforesaid letter of credit in priority; 3. That Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin assume joint and several liability for repayment of the aforesaid debts to be borne by Lanyue Energy; 4. That Yuedong Electric Power and Blue Sea Shipping, from March 6, 2013, pay a penalty for breach of contract calculated at a daily rate of 0.05% on the amount they are obligated to pay to CCB Liwan Branch for assuming guarantee liability until all amounts are fully paid; 5. That CCB Liwan Branch's right to be paid in priority over the 6% equity interest held by Lan Wenbin in Lanyue Energy be confirmed; 6. That Lanyue Energy, Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin bear all litigation costs of this case and the necessary expenses incurred by CCB Liwan Branch for realizing the aforesaid claims.

The Guangzhou Intermediate Court, after trial, found the following facts: On December 5, 2011, CCB Liwan Branch and Lanyue Energy entered into the "Trade Finance Facility Contract" numbered 2011 Li Mao E No. 011 and related appendices, stipulating that from December 22, 2011, to November 25, 2012, CCB Liwan Branch would provide Lanyue Energy with a trade finance facility not exceeding the equivalent of RMB 550 million, including the issuance of usance letters of credit with a maturity of 90 days (inclusive) or less and a facility amount equivalent to RMB 550 million. On December 5, 2011, CCB Liwan Branch (Party B) separately entered into the "Maximum Guarantee Contracts" numbered 2011 Li Zui Gao E No. 035 and 2011 Li Zui Gao E No. 036, and the "Maximum Natural Person Guarantee Contract" numbered 2011 Li Zi Bao No. 070, with Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin (Party A), stipulating: Party A would provide a joint and several liability guarantee with a maximum limit of RMB 2.67 billion for the debts under the aforesaid Lanyue Energy trade finance contract. The scope of guarantee included all debts under the principal contract, including but not limited to all principal, interest (including compound interest and penalty interest), liquidated damages, compensation, other amounts payable by the debtor to Party B (including but not limited to relevant handling fees, telecommunication fees, miscellaneous fees advanced by Party B, relevant bank fees that the beneficiary under the letter of credit refuses to bear, etc.), and expenses incurred by Party B for realizing the claims and security rights (including but not limited to litigation fees, arbitration fees, property preservation fees, travel expenses, enforcement fees, appraisal fees, auction fees, notarization fees, service fees, announcement fees, attorney fees, etc.). The contract also stipulated: If the debts under the principal contract become due or Party B declares the debts accelerated due pursuant to the provisions of the principal contract or the law, and the debtor fails to perform in full and on time, or the debtor breaches other provisions of the principal contract, Party A shall assume guarantee liability within the scope of the guarantee. If Party A fails to pay all amounts due within the time limit requested by Party B, Party A shall, from the date of delay to the date Party A pays all amounts due to Party B, pay a penalty for breach of contract to Party B at a daily rate of 0.05% on the delayed payment amount. Under such circumstances, the sum of the guarantee liability assumed by Party A and the aforesaid penalty shall not be limited by the maximum liability limit stipulated in the contract.

On November 2, 2012, Lanyue Energy applied to CCB Liwan Branch for the issuance of a usance letter of credit with a trade finance facility of RMB 85.92 million. Simultaneously, for the purpose of applying for the issuance of the aforesaid letter of credit, Lanyue Energy issued a "Trust Receipt" to CCB Liwan Branch and entered into the "Margin Pledge Contract" numbered 2012 Li Zhi No. 185. The "Trust Receipt" confirmed that, from the date of issuance of the receipt, CCB Liwan Branch acquired ownership of the documents and goods involved under the aforesaid letter of credit, that a trust legal relationship was established between CCB Liwan Branch and Lanyue Energy, with CCB Liwan Branch as the settlor and beneficiary, and Lanyue Energy as the trustee of the aforesaid trust goods. The "Margin Pledge Contract" stipulated that Lanyue Energy pay a margin of RMB 9.5 million, and later an additional margin of RMB 310,000, to provide pledge guarantee for the aforesaid debts. CCB Liwan Branch, on November 2, 2012, issued a documentary letter of credit numbered 44016010002089 for Lanyue Energy and sent a "Notice of Issuance of Letter of Credit" to Lanyue Energy. After the letter of credit was issued, Lanyue Energy imported 164,998 tons of coal. Subsequently, CCB Liwan Branch accepted the letter of credit and disbursed RMB 84,867,952.27 to Lanyue Energy, for Lanyue Energy to repay the advance payment under the letter of credit of the Seoul Branch of China Construction Bank. Lanyue Energy failed to fully repay the debt when it became due, constituting a breach of contract.

On December 6, 2012, CCB Liwan Branch and Lan Wenbin entered into the "Maximum Pledge of Rights Contract" numbered 2012 Li Zui Gao E Zhi No. 018, stipulating that Lan Wenbin, with his 6% equity interest in Lanyue Energy, would provide a maximum pledge of rights guarantee for the debts under the loan contracts entered into between CCB Liwan Branch, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lanyue Energy from January 1, 2008, to December 31, 2012, regarding multiple credit facilities such as loans and bank acceptances. The maximum limit of guarantee liability under the maximum pledge of rights was RMB 2,389,780,200. On December 7, 2012, the Guangdong Provincial Administration for Industry and Commerce registered the aforesaid equity pledge.

On March 21 and April 21, 2013, CCB Liwan Branch twice sent "Overdue Loan (Advance) Demand Notices" to Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin, demanding that Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin perform their guarantee liability and repay the principal amount of RMB 84,867,952.27 and interest of RMB 551,641.69 owed by Lanyue Energy. Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin failed to repay the aforesaid amounts.

It was also found that the delivery order for the 164,998 tons of coal imported by Lanyue Energy was delivered by Lanyue Energy to CCB Liwan Branch. However, due to other disputes, this batch of coal was sealed up by the Fangchenggang Port District People's Court of Guangxi. CCB Liwan Branch raised an objection regarding the preservative seizure to the Beihai Maritime Court of Guangxi, and the objection was still under trial. Because the coal was sealed up by the court, CCB Liwan Branch was unable to take delivery and realize the proceeds.

CCB Liwan Branch failed to submit evidence of expenses incurred for realizing the claims during the trial, stating that such expenses had not yet been incurred.

The Guangzhou Intermediate Court clarified the requests filed by CCB Liwan Branch and requested it to clarify its claims. CCB Liwan Branch insisted on its claims.

The Guangzhou Intermediate Court, after trial, held: CCB Liwan Branch requested that Lanyue Energy and the guarantors repay the advance payment and corresponding interest, and also requested confirmation of its ownership and priority right over the 164,998 tons of coal under the documentary letter of credit, and that the guarantors bear liability for a daily penalty of 0.05% for failure to perform the guarantee obligation. Lanyue Energy, Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin, however, argued that the bill of lading for the goods had been delivered to CCB Liwan Branch, that they had performed their repayment obligation, and thus no further repayment obligation existed; that the guarantors could only assume liability within the scope provided by law, and requiring the guarantors to assume guarantee liability beyond that statutory scope lacked legal basis. The issues in dispute in this case are: 1. The issue of ownership of the 164,998 tons of coal; 2. Whether CCB Liwan Branch, if it does not have ownership of the 164,998 tons of coal, has a right to be paid in priority; 3. Whether Lanyue Energy should repay the principal of RMB 84,867,952.27 and interest advanced by CCB Liwan Branch; 4. Whether Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin should bear the liability for a daily penalty of 0.05%.

Regarding the ownership of the 164,998 tons of coal. Due to the issuance of the letter of credit, a creditor-debtor relationship arose between CCB Liwan Branch and Lanyue Energy. While requesting a judgment that Lanyue Energy and the guarantors repay the advance payment, CCB Liwan Branch also requested confirmation of ownership of the 164,998 tons of coal. This not only involves two different legal relationships being asserted in the same case, but would also result in CCB Liwan Branch being doubly benefited from the same legal fact, and moreover, these two claims are inherently contradictory. In this case, CCB Liwan Branch did not dispute with Lanyue Energy, Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin over the ownership of the 164,998 tons of coal. After the coal was sealed up by another court, CCB Liwan Branch had also sought other relief measures to resolve the matter. The request of CCB Liwan Branch to confirm the ownership of the 164,998 tons of coal does not fall within the scope of trial of this case, and its claim in this regard should be dismissed.

Regarding whether CCB Liwan Branch has a right to be paid in priority over the 164,998 tons of coal. CCB Liwan Branch argued that Lanyue Energy had delivered the bill of lading for the 164,998 tons of coal to CCB Liwan Branch, and the parties had also signed the "Trust Agreement," and that the bill of lading actually had the nature of a pledge, so CCB Liwan Branch had a right to be paid in priority over the 164,998 tons of coal. Although CCB Liwan Branch holds the bill of lading for the 164,998 tons of coal, CCB Liwan Branch and Lanyue Energy did not set up a pledge on the bill of lading in accordance with legal procedures. Even if the trust receipt and delivery of the bill of lading had the meaning of providing security for the debts in this case, their effect is limited to the parties themselves and does not produce effect against third parties. The claim of CCB Liwan Branch for confirmation of its right to be paid in priority over the 164,998 tons of coal is not supported.

Regarding whether Lanyue Energy should repay the principal of RMB 84,867,952.27 and interest advanced by CCB Liwan Branch. Lanyue Energy argued that it had delivered the bill of lading for the 164,998 tons of coal to CCB Liwan Branch to offset the amounts owed by Lanyue Energy, and that the value of the 164,998 tons of coal was sufficient to offset the principal and interest of the debts involved in this case, so CCB Liwan Branch should not further require Lanyue Energy, Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin to bear repayment and guarantee liability; even if repayment was required, CCB Liwan Branch should first realize the 164,998 tons of coal, and Lanyue Energy, Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin should only repay the shortfall. Although Lanyue Energy delivered the bill of lading for the 164,998 tons of coal to CCB Liwan Branch, the parties did not agree to directly offset the debt with the coal. Moreover, it was not determined whether the bill of lading was a clean bill of lading, whether CCB Liwan Branch could take delivery of the goods against the bill of lading to offset the debt, and other matters. According to the facts found, due to other debt disputes, the coal under the bill of lading had been sealed up by the relevant court, CCB Liwan Branch did not actually take delivery of the coal, and its claims were not realized. Lanyue Energy, Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin confirmed the principal and interest amounts owed to CCB Liwan Branch, and CCB Liwan Branch has the right to require Lanyue Energy to repay the principal amount of RMB 84,867,952.27 and interest advanced. As for the method by which the debt is to be repaid and how the bill of lading is to be dealt with, the parties may negotiate on their own. Therefore, CCB Liwan Branch's request that Lanyue Energy repay the principal of RMB 84,867,952.27 and interest advanced, and that Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin assume joint and several liability for repayment of the aforesaid claims, is supported.

Regarding whether Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin should bear the liability for a daily penalty of 0.05%. Although the guarantee contracts entered into between CCB Liwan Branch and Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin stipulated that if the guarantors failed to perform the repayment obligation when due, they would bear liability for a daily penalty of 0.05%, and that after the principal debtor Lanyue Energy failed to perform the repayment obligation when due, CCB Liwan Branch also demanded performance from the guarantors. However, given that Lanyue Energy, when entering into the contract with CCB Liwan Branch, delivered the bill of lading for the coal under the letter of credit to CCB Liwan Branch, there existed an expression of intention between the parties to repay the debt with the proceeds from the realization of the coal. Now, due to a third party's reason, the coal cannot be taken delivery of, and there is still a dispute between the parties regarding the amount of the creditor-debtor rights and obligations to be performed. It is inappropriate for CCB Liwan Branch to demand that Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin bear liability for a daily penalty of 0.05% on the ground that they have already constituted a breach of contract. Furthermore, the principal of RMB 84,867,952.27 and interest that CCB Liwan Branch requested Lanyue Energy to repay in its lawsuit already included compound interest and penalty interest. Lanyue Energy, Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin had no objection to the principal and interest amounts. This amount constituted compensation for the loss of principal and interest of CCB Liwan Branch. On this basis, requiring the guarantors to further bear a daily penalty of 0.05% would undoubtedly increase the guarantors' liability and constitute a double penalty on the guarantors, which does not comply with the provision of Article 113 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China that "the amount of compensation for loss shall be equivalent to the loss caused by the breach of contract." Therefore, CCB Liwan Branch's claim in this regard is not supported.

Regarding CCB Liwan Branch's request for a right to be paid in priority over the 6% equity interest held by Lan Wenbin in Lanyue Energy. Because the pledge of rights was legally established through lawful registration, and CCB Liwan Branch, Lanyue Energy, and Lan Wenbin had no objection, this is supported.

In summary, CCB Liwan Branch's reasons for requesting that Lanyue Energy and its guarantors Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin repay the principal of RMB 84,867,952.27 and interest, and that CCB Liwan Branch has a right to be paid in priority over the 6% equity interest held by Lan Wenbin in Lanyue Energy, are established and are supported. CCB Liwan Branch's requests for confirmation of ownership and priority right over the 164,998 tons of coal, and for Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin to bear liability for a daily penalty of 0.05% from the date of overdue payment within the scope of the guarantee amount the guarantors should bear, have no merit and are dismissed. In accordance with Articles 8, 107, 113, 206, and 207 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, Articles 6, 18, 21, 31, and 78 of the Guarantee Law of the People's Republic of China, and Articles 134 and 142 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Guangzhou Intermediate Court rendered the following judgment: 1. Within ten days from the date this judgment becomes legally effective, Lanyue Energy shall repay to CCB Liwan Branch the principal of the letter of credit advance payment in the amount of RMB 84,867,952.27 and interest up to the date of repayment determined by the judgment (interest tentatively calculated up to March 21, 2013, is RMB 551,641.70; interest from March 22, 2013, to the date of repayment determined by the judgment shall be calculated at a daily rate of 0.05%); 2. Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin shall assume joint and several liability for repayment of the aforesaid debts. After Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin assume liability, they shall have the right to recourse against Lanyue Energy; 3. CCB Liwan Branch shall have the right to be paid in priority over the 6% equity interest held by Lan Wenbin in Lanyue Energy; 4. Other claims of CCB Liwan Branch are dismissed. The court acceptance fee for the first instance of RMB 473,898 and the preservation fee of RMB 5,000 shall be borne jointly by Lanyue Energy, Yuedong Electric Power, Blue Sea Shipping, and Lan Wenbin.

China Construction Bank Liwan Sub-branch, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, filed an appeal with the Guangdong High People's Court, requesting that the first, second, and third items of the first-instance judgment be upheld, that the fourth item be overturned, and that all claims made in the first instance be supported.

The Guangdong High People's Court confirmed the facts found by the first-instance court.

The Guangdong High People's Court held that this case is a letter of credit financing dispute. Based on the parties' appeal and response opinions, the issues in dispute at the second instance were threefold: first, whether CCB Liwan Sub-branch had ownership of the 164,998 tons of coal involved; second, whether CCB Liwan Sub-branch had a priority right to repayment from the 164,998 tons of coal involved; third, whether Yuedong Electric Power, Lanhai Shipping, and Lan Wenbin should bear liability for liquidated damages at the rate of five ten-thousandths per day.

Regarding the issue of whether CCB Liwan Sub-branch had ownership of the 164,998 tons of coal involved. CCB Liwan Sub-branch filed a lawsuit requesting confirmation of its ownership of the coal under the bill of lading it held. After the batch of coal was sealed up by another court, CCB Liwan Sub-branch raised an objection to the court's sealing up but did not file a lawsuit to confirm ownership. Therefore, the first-instance judgment's conclusion that CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim for confirmation of ownership did not fall within the scope of this case's trial lacked a sufficient basis and should be corrected. Article 23 of the Property Law of the PRC provides that the creation and transfer of real rights in movables shall take effect upon delivery. When Lanyue Energy issued the Trust Receipt, the coal involved was in the possession of the carrier for transport, constituting a situation of possession by a third party. In the absence of direct delivery, only the form of constructive delivery under Article 26 of the Property Law of the PRC could be adopted. Article 71 of the Maritime Code of the PRC provides that a bill of lading is a document used to prove the contract of carriage of goods by sea and that the goods have been received or loaded by the carrier, and the carrier undertakes to deliver the goods against it. Delivery of a bill of lading only signifies the transfer of the right to demand delivery of the goods. Without notifying the actual possessor of the transfer of the right to demand delivery, it does not constitute delivery of the goods under the bill of lading. In this case, CCB Liwan Sub-branch did not provide sufficient evidence to prove that it had notified the carrier, who actually possessed the goods, of the fact of the goods transfer to complete delivery. Therefore, CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim for ownership of the coal involved lacked a sufficient basis and was not supported. The first-instance judgment's dismissal of CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim on this ground was not improper in terms of the outcome and should be upheld.

Regarding the issue of whether CCB Liwan Sub-branch had a priority right to repayment from the 164,998 tons of coal involved. Article 7 of the Trust Law of the PRC provides that trust property must be property lawfully owned by the trustor. From the content of the Trust Receipt, the trust property was the coal involved. CCB Liwan Sub-branch, as the trustor, had not obtained ownership of the coal involved, so the trust with the coal involved as trust property was not validly established. Article 112 of the Property Law of the PRC provides that a pledge right shall be created upon delivery of the pledged property by the pledgor. The creation of a pledge over movables requires the pledgor to deliver the pledged property. According to Article 88 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Security Law of the PRC, if a pledgor pledges property in indirect possession, the pledge contract shall be deemed to be delivered when the written notice is served on the possessor. Although the Trust Receipt contained a clause regarding the use of proceeds from the disposal of the coal involved to repay CCB Liwan Sub-branch's loan, and Lanyue Energy delivered the bill of lading to CCB Liwan Sub-branch, there was no evidence proving that CCB Liwan Sub-branch or Lanyue Energy notified the carrier of the creation of a pledge over the coal involved. Therefore, CCB Liwan Sub-branch did not have a pledge right over the coal involved. In summary, the first-instance judgment's dismissal of CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim for a priority right to repayment from the coal involved was well-founded and should be upheld.

Regarding the issue of whether Yuedong Electric Power, Lanhai Shipping, and Lan Wenbin should bear liability for liquidated damages at the rate of five ten-thousandths per day. Because Yuedong Electric Power, Lanhai Shipping, and Lan Wenbin raised the defense in their first-instance responses that "the guarantee liability should be a liability within the scope of the guarantor's guarantee, and guarantee liability exceeding the guarantor's guarantee scope has no legal basis," this was deemed as having raised a defense that the liquidated damages were excessive. Given that the interest claimed by CCB Liwan Sub-branch in its lawsuit against Lanyue Energy for repayment already included compound interest and penalty interest, and it simultaneously demanded that the guarantors bear joint and several liability for the above principal and interest and also pay liquidated damages at the rate of five ten-thousandths per day, this constituted a double penalty against the guarantors. Therefore, the first-instance judgment's dismissal of CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim for liquidated damages at the rate of five ten-thousandths per day from Yuedong Electric Power, Lanhai Shipping, and Lan Wenbin was not improper and should be upheld.

In summary, the first-instance judgment found the facts clearly and the outcome was not improper. CCB Liwan Sub-branch's appeal claims and reasons lacked sufficient basis and should be dismissed in accordance with law. The Guangdong High People's Court, pursuant to Article 170, Paragraph 1, Item 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, rendered the following judgment: appeal dismissed, the original judgment affirmed. The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 1,921.69 shall be borne by CCB Liwan Sub-branch.

CCB Liwan Sub-branch, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, applied to this Court for retrial, still requesting a judgment supporting all its claims raised in the first instance. The main facts and reasons were: First, the bill of lading under the letter of credit involved was a bearer order bill of lading, which in nature constitutes a document of title. CCB Liwan Sub-branch, having accepted and entrusted an overseas reimbursing bank to make payment, lawfully held the documents including the bill of lading under the letter of credit, and thus had ownership of the goods represented by the bill of lading. Second, CCB Liwan Sub-branch's ultimate purpose in claiming ownership of the coal was to obtain priority satisfaction of its creditor's rights from the proceeds of the coal disposal, with any shortfall to be further satisfied by Lanyue Energy, and there was no double recovery. Third, in the alternative, even if CCB Liwan Sub-branch did not have ownership of the goods involved, it had a priority right to repayment. In this case, the Trust Receipt issued by Lanyue Energy to CCB Liwan Sub-branch was in the nature of a pledge contract. Where Lanyue Energy had delivered the bill of lading to CCB Liwan Sub-branch, according to Article 224 of the Property Law of the PRC, which provides that a pledge over rights is created when the document of title is delivered to the pledgee, a pledge over the bill of lading should be deemed to have been created, and CCB Liwan Sub-branch had a priority right to repayment from the goods under the bill of lading. The original second-instance judgment erroneously treated the pledge in this case as a pledge over movables and, applying the provisions of the Property Law concerning pledges over movables, held that CCB Liwan Sub-branch did not have a pledge right, thereby dismissing CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim for a priority right to repayment from the goods involved, which was an error in the application of law. Fourth, in the maximum-amount guarantee contracts signed between Yuedong Electric Power and Lanhai Shipping respectively with CCB Liwan Sub-branch, it was clearly agreed that if the guarantor failed to pay all amounts due within the period requested by the creditor, it should pay liquidated damages to CCB Liwan Sub-branch from the overdue date at the rate of five ten-thousandths per day. Yuedong Electric Power and Lanhai Shipping did not raise a defense that the liquidated damages were excessive and requested a reduction. The court directly dismissed CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim for liquidated damages on the ground that they were excessive, which was also an error in the application of law.

Lanyue Energy and Lan Wenbin responded, arguing: First, according to the Trust Receipt, CCB Liwan Sub-branch should have delivered the relevant documents to Lanyue Energy. CCB Liwan Sub-branch failed to perform its obligation to deliver the documents, breaching the contract first. Its claim for Lanyue Energy to bear liability for breach and for the relevant guarantors to assume guarantee liability lacked legal basis. Second, CCB Liwan Sub-branch still held the documents including the bill of lading under the letter of credit and could take delivery of the goods involved against the bill of lading. In this situation, its claim against Lanyue Energy and the relevant guarantors also lacked legal basis. In summary, it requested that CCB Liwan Sub-branch's application for retrial be dismissed.

Lanhai Shipping responded, arguing: First, CCB Liwan Sub-branch failed to perform its obligation to deliver the documents according to the Trust Receipt, breaching the contract first. Its claim for Lanhai Shipping to assume guarantee liability lacked legal basis. Second, the interest claimed by CCB Liwan Sub-branch in its lawsuit against Lanyue Energy for repayment already included compound interest and penalty interest. To demand additionally that Lanhai Shipping bear liability for liquidated damages at the rate of five ten-thousandths per day constituted an excessive assertion of rights and should not be supported. In summary, it requested that CCB Liwan Sub-branch's application for retrial be dismissed.

Yuedong Electric Power did not respond.

With the exception of CCB Liwan Sub-branch's objections to the facts concerning the circulation process of the bill of lading, the parties had no objection to the facts found by the original trial courts, and this Court confirms them.

This Court further finds: The Trade Financing Facility Contract signed by CCB Liwan Sub-branch and Lanyue Energy on December 5, 2011 contained an appendix entitled "Special Agreement on the Issuance of Letters of Credit," which formed an integral part of the Trade Financing Facility Contract. Article 9, paragraph 2 of the "Special Agreement on the Issuance of Letters of Credit" provided that if Party A (Lanyue Energy) committed a breach or one of the circumstances that might jeopardize Party B's (CCB Liwan Sub-branch's) claims under the Trade Financing Facility Contract occurred, Party B had the right to exercise one or more of the following rights: (1) if Party B made a payment, from the date of payment, Party B had the right to charge overdue interest at the overdue loan interest rate, to be specifically agreed upon by the parties when handling the individual transaction; (2) for amounts payable by Party A, Party B had the right to directly deduct from the margin account opened by Party A with Party B, or from other accounts opened by Party A with the China Construction Bank system, or from other accounts receivable of Party A; (3) dispose of the documents and/or goods under the letter of credit; (4) exercise security rights; (5) require Party A to add margin or other security acceptable to Party B; (6) other remedial measures agreed in the Trade Financing Facility Contract; (7) other measures permitted by law.

On October 23, 2012, the master of the vessel RANNEL DE LA PUERTA issued a bill of lading to XSTRATA COAL MARKETING AG, with the "consignee" field showing "TO ORDER." On December 6, 2012, CCB Liwan Sub-branch received the full set of documents including the bill of lading involved sent by the beneficiary through Bank of China (Hong Kong) Limited. CCB Liwan Sub-branch informed Lanyue Energy of the contents of the documents under the letter of credit via a "Notice of Letter of Credit Documents." Lanyue Energy expressly accepted the documents and undertook to make payment on March 6, 2013. Thereafter, CCB Liwan Sub-branch entrusted China Construction Bank Corporation Seoul Branch to pay the amount under the letter of credit, USD 15,226,015.44, on December 14, 2012. After the payment deadline under the letter of credit expired, Lanyue Energy did not pay the full amount due to CCB Liwan Sub-branch.

This Court further finds that on November 2, 2012, Lanyue Energy issued a Trust Receipt to CCB Liwan Sub-branch, the preamble of which stated: "Whereas your bank and this company have entered into the Trade Financing Facility Contract numbered 2011 Li Mao E 011 and/or the Trust Receipt Loan Contract numbered /, this company hereby issues this Trust Receipt to your bank, and this Trust Receipt is an integral part of the above contracts. Once your bank delivers to this company, or consents to this company's use/disposal of, the goods or the documents of title, documents, etc. under the letter of credit/import collection/import documents against payment (T/T) with business number 44016010002089, the corresponding rights and obligations between this company and your bank shall be determined in accordance with the following content." The Trust Receipt also stipulated that a trust legal relationship would be established between CCB Liwan Sub-branch and Lanyue Energy, with CCB Liwan Sub-branch as the trustor and beneficiary, acquiring ownership of the above documents and the goods they represented from the date of issuance of the Trust Receipt; Lanyue Energy, as the trustee, had the right to handle the trust property including the aforementioned documents and the goods they represented. CCB Liwan Sub-branch received the above Trust Receipt issued by Lanyue Energy, but after obtaining the bill of lading involved in December 2012, due to a sharp decline in energy market prices and the deterioration of Lanyue Energy's business condition, it did not deliver the bill of lading and other relevant documents to Lanyue Energy as required by the Trust Receipt. The coal under the bill of lading arrived at the port in December 2012. In April 2013, Beihai Fangchenggang Port Group Co., Ltd. applied to the Beihai Maritime Court for pre-litigation preservation on the ground that Lanyue Energy owed it yard storage fees. The Beihai Maritime Court, upon application, sealed up 609,625.5 tons of coal belonging to Lanyue Energy, including the 164,998 tons of coal involved. CCB Liwan Sub-branch submitted an objection to the property preservation to the Beihai Maritime Court, requesting an immediate lifting of the seal. In two cases filed by Fangchenggang Port Group Co., Ltd. against Lanyue Energy, after the judgments of the relevant courts became effective, the Beihai Maritime Court issued rulings [(2014) Bei Hai Fa Zhi Zi No. 54 and 55] ordering the auction of the 609,625.5 tons of coal including the coal under the bill of lading involved, but both auctions ended in failure. On July 25, 2014, CCB Liwan Sub-branch filed an execution objection with the Beihai Maritime Court, which has not yet made a ruling on the objection as of the date of this judgment.

After this Court publicly heard the case and deliberated, but before the service of the judgment, on July 23, 2015, the Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court issued civil rulings [(2014) Sui Zhong Fa Min Po Zi No. 1-1 and (2014) Sui Zhong Fa Min Po Zi No. 9-1] accepting the bankruptcy liquidation applications filed by Nanchang Bank Co., Ltd. Guangzhou Branch against Lanyue Energy and Lanhai Shipping respectively. On August 17, 2015, the same court issued civil decisions [(2014) Sui Zhong Fa Min Po Zi No. 1-2 and (2014) Sui Zhong Fa Min Po Zi No. 9-2] appointing Beijing Dacheng (Guangzhou) Law Firm as the administrator for both cases, with Jiang Bin as the responsible person. In accordance with relevant provisions, this Court changed the legal representative of Lanyue Energy and Lanhai Shipping from Lan Wenbin to the litigation representative Jiang Bin.

This Court holds that, based on the parties' applications for retrial and responses, the main issues in dispute are threefold: first, whether CCB Liwan Sub-branch has ownership of the goods under the bill of lading involved; second, whether CCB Liwan Sub-branch has a priority right to repayment from the proceeds derived from the disposal of the goods involved; third, whether Yuedong Electric Power and Lanhai Shipping should additionally bear liability for liquidated damages at the rate of five ten-thousandths per day.

I. Whether CCB Liwan Sub-branch has ownership of the goods under the bill of lading involved

CCB Liwan Sub-branch claims that a bill of lading is a document of title and that it is the lawful holder of the bill of lading, therefore it has ownership of the goods involved. In response to CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim, two issues need to be addressed: first, whether a bill of lading is a document of title; second, if a bill of lading is a document of title, does holding the bill of lading automatically confer ownership of the goods under the bill of lading.

Regarding the issue of whether a bill of lading is a document of title. Article 71 of the Maritime Code of the PRC provides that a bill of lading is a document used to prove the contract of carriage of goods by sea and that the goods have been received or loaded by the carrier, and the carrier undertakes to deliver the goods against it. According to this provision, the bill of lading is both evidence of the existence of the contract of carriage and a document by which the carrier undertakes to deliver the goods. Furthermore, pursuant to Article 78, paragraph 1 of the Maritime Code of the PRC, which provides that the rights and obligations between the carrier and the consignee or holder of the bill of lading shall be determined by the terms of the bill of lading, the holder of the bill of lading enjoys the right to claim the creditor's rights stated in the bill of lading, that is, the bill of lading is a document evidencing the holder's right to claim delivery of the goods from the carrier, a right in the nature of a claim. In this sense, the bill of lading is a document of title in terms of the right to claim. Meanwhile, in a contract of carriage of goods by sea, the owner of the goods, after delivering them to the carrier and having them actually possessed by the carrier, does not lose ownership. Since the owner still has ownership of the goods, it certainly can, based on that ownership, request the carrier to return the goods. This is a right to claim the return of the original thing arising from ownership, which falls within the category of real rights. The bill of lading is the sole document for taking delivery of the goods from the carrier, and it naturally can represent the right to claim the return of the original thing arising from the ownership of the goods. In this sense, the bill of lading is also a document of title. It can be seen that the bill of lading has dual attributes: it is both a document evidencing a right to claim and a document of title. Article 3, paragraph 1 of the Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in Cases Involving Delivery of Goods without an Original Bill of Lading provides: "If a carrier delivers goods without an original bill of lading, causing loss to the holder of the original bill of lading, the holder of the original bill of lading may demand that the carrier bear liability for breach of contract or liability for tort." The reason the holder of the bill of lading can demand the carrier bear liability for breach of contract is based on the bill of lading's attribute as a document evidencing a right to claim; the holder is the creditor enjoying the rights stated in the bill of lading. The reason the holder can demand the carrier bear liability for tort is based on the bill of lading's attribute as a document of title; the holder is the owner of the goods under the bill of lading or a person with a real right established on the basis of ownership. Clearly, this judicial interpretation also recognizes that the bill of lading has dual attributes as a document of title and a document evidencing a right to claim.

Regarding whether holding a bill of lading confers ownership of the goods under the bill of lading. Under Article 79 of the Maritime Code of the PRC, bills of lading are divided into straight bills of lading, order bills of lading, and bearer bills of lading. Straight bills of lading are non-negotiable, while order bills of lading may be transferred by endorsement, and bearer bills of lading may be transferred without endorsement. For a non-negotiable straight bill of lading, only the person named on the bill of lading has the right to claim delivery of the goods and the right to claim in rem. However, for negotiable order bills of lading and bearer bills of lading that are transferred to others for possession, whether the holder of the bill of lading automatically acquires the right to claim delivery and the right to claim in rem represented by the bill of lading, or in other words, whether whoever holds the bill of lading automatically owns the goods under the bill of lading, cannot be generalized and should be specifically analyzed based on different circumstances. The bill of lading itself represents both the right to claim in personam and the right to claim in rem, and even serves as a document of title; this merely indicates the functions and attributes of the bill of lading. For the carrier, generally speaking, the bill of lading is the sole certificate and basis for deciding whether to release the goods; upon sight of the bill of lading, the carrier may release the goods, and moreover, should release the goods upon sight. Whether the holder has a legal reason or basis, and what legal reason or basis underlies the holding of the bill of lading, need not be examined or inquired into. However, for the holder of the bill of lading, to legally and properly exercise the rights under the bill of lading against the carrier, there must be a legal reason or basis, that is, the existence of a certain legal relationship as a prerequisite. The same delivery of a bill of lading may be based on a custodial relationship for the bill of lading, a sale of goods relationship, a relationship for establishing a pledge of rights under the bill of lading or a pledge of movable property under the bill of lading, etc. Based on different legal relationships, the holder of the bill of lading enjoys different rights. If it is merely based on a custodial legal relationship for the bill of lading, the holder can certainly demand delivery of the goods from the carrier by presenting the bill of lading, but if it claims ownership or other property rights over the goods, it would obviously lack legality and legitimacy. In the case of a sale of goods relationship, delivering the bill of lading constitutes a transfer of the right to claim in personam and the right to claim in rem represented by the bill of lading, constituting constructive delivery as provided in Article 26 of the Property Law of the PRC, and produces the legal effect of transferring ownership of the goods under the bill of lading. In the case of establishing a pledge of rights under the bill of lading, delivering the bill of lading produces the legal effect of establishing a pledge of rights under the bill of lading. That is to say, although the delivery of the bill of lading can produce the legal effect of a change in property rights over the goods under the bill of lading just like the delivery of the goods themselves, whether the holder acquires property rights upon receiving delivery of the bill of lading and what type of property rights it acquires depends on the terms of the contract on which it is based. The same logic applies to the delivery of movable property: whether the possessor of movable property, upon receiving delivery of the movable property, enjoys ownership, a pledge of movable property, or possession based on a contractual relationship depends on the agreement between the parties in the contract.

In this case, it is undisputed that CCB Liwan Sub-branch holds the bill of lading, but whether it enjoys ownership of the goods under the bill of lading, as analyzed above, depends on the agreement between it and Lanyue Energy in the relevant contract. If CCB Liwan Sub-branch legally holds the bill of lading based on an agreement to purchase the goods or transfer ownership of the goods, then it is the owner. If it is based on an agreement to establish a pledge of movable property or a pledge of rights, then it is the pledgee. Neither the Trade Financing Facility Agreement entered into between CCB Liwan Sub-branch and Lanyue Energy on December 5, 2011, nor the Special Agreement on Opening Letters of Credit, contains any provision regarding CCB Liwan Sub-branch's ownership of the goods under the bill of lading in the event Lanyue Energy fails to pay for and take delivery of the documents. The Trust Receipt issued by Lanyue Energy to CCB Liwan Sub-branch on November 2, 2012, states that once CCB Liwan Sub-branch delivers to Lanyue Energy or agrees to Lanyue Energy's use of the goods under the letter of credit or the documents such as title documents, from the date of issuance of this receipt, CCB Liwan Sub-branch acquires ownership of the documents and goods under the letter of credit. According to the above content of the Trust Receipt, although CCB Liwan Sub-branch holds the bill of lading, it does not automatically enjoy ownership of the goods under the bill of lading. Only when CCB Liwan Sub-branch delivers the bill of lading or the goods under the bill of lading to Lanyue Energy for disposal does Lanyue Energy transfer ownership of the goods under the bill of lading. In fact, CCB Liwan Sub-branch did not deliver the bill of lading or the goods under the bill of lading to Lanyue Energy for disposal, so the Trust Receipt certainly cannot serve as the contractual basis for it to acquire ownership of the goods under the bill of lading. Therefore, CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim that "the bill of lading is a document of title, and having legally held the bill of lading, it enjoys ownership of the goods under the bill of lading" lacks factual and legal basis, and is not supported by this Court. CCB Liwan Sub-branch also argued that the ultimate purpose of claiming ownership of the goods under the bill of lading is to satisfy the claim arising from the letter of credit advance payment with priority from the proceeds of disposing of the goods, and any shortfall would be further satisfied by Lanyue Energy. From this, it can be seen that its intention is to secure the realization of its claim through the form of Lanyue Energy transferring ownership of the goods under the bill of lading. However: First, the relevant contracts do not contain a specific and clear provision as claimed by CCB Liwan Sub-branch, namely "to use the proceeds from the disposal of the goods of which it claims ownership to satisfy the letter of credit advance payment with priority, and any shortfall to be further satisfied by Lanyue Energy"; this claim lacks a contractual basis. Second, even if there were a corresponding contractual provision, China's current laws do not provide for a type of security interest where ownership of movable property is transferred to secure a claim. According to the principle of numerus clausus of property rights under the Property Law, it cannot produce the effect of a property right, so how can there be priority in satisfaction? Without a contractual basis and without a legal basis, if this Court were to find that CCB Liwan Sub-branch owns the goods under the bill of lading while also requiring Lanyue Energy to pay all amounts due under the letter of credit, it would result in double recovery. The first-instance original judgment dismissed this claim by CCB Liwan Sub-branch on the ground that its claim would result in double recovery, though the reasoning was not sufficiently thorough, it was not without reason. The second-instance original judgment, based on Article 71 of the Maritime Code of the PRC, held that "the delivery of a bill of lading merely means the transfer of the right to demand delivery of the goods, and does not constitute delivery of the goods under the bill of lading until the fact of the transfer of the right to demand delivery has been notified to the actual possessor." However, according to Article 26 of the Property Law of the PRC, constructive delivery does not require notification to the third party actually possessing the movable property as a necessary condition for completing the delivery. Even if the bill of lading only has the attribute of a document of title in personam, by reference to Article 80(1) of the Contract Law of the PRC, which provides that "if a creditor assigns its rights, it shall notify the debtor; without such notification, the assignment is not effective against the debtor," at the time of delivery of the bill of lading, the transfer of the right to claim in personam can take effect, thereby completing the constructive delivery of the goods under the bill of lading. However, without notification, the transfer of the right to claim in personam cannot be effective against the actual possessor of the goods under the bill of lading, but it cannot be concluded that "delivery of the goods under the bill of lading does not occur." Moreover, the bills of lading involved in this case are negotiable order bills of lading, and it is only foreseeable by the actual possessor of the goods, i.e., the carrier, that the holder of the bill of lading has a claim by virtue of the bill of lading, and no notification is required. Therefore, the above reasoning of the second-instance original judgment applied the law incorrectly and should be corrected, but the result of this part of the ruling is not improper and should be affirmed.

Furthermore, based on the content of the Trust Receipt, Lanyue Energy, Lanhai Shipping, and Lan Wenbin argued that CCB Liwan Sub-branch's failure to deliver the bill of lading to Lanyue Energy constituted a breach of contract first, and therefore Lanyue Energy should not bear liability for breach of contract, and Lanhai Shipping and Lan Wenbin should not bear guarantee liability either. However, according to the terms of the letter of credit contract and its annexes, Lanyue Energy is obligated to pay the amounts due under the letter of credit upon maturity, and CCB Liwan Sub-branch is obligated to release the documents only after Lanyue Energy has paid; it has no obligation to release the documents first. Even if, as stated in the Trust Receipt, CCB Liwan Sub-branch should first deliver the bill of lading or the goods under the bill of lading to Lanyue Energy, CCB Liwan Sub-branch's failure to do so would merely mean that the effect of securing CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim through the form of transferring ownership of the goods does not arise; it cannot thereby exempt Lanyue Energy from its payment obligations under the letter of credit or the guarantee liabilities of Lanhai Shipping and Lan Wenbin. Moreover, Lanyue Energy's operating conditions have significantly deteriorated due to factors in the energy market, and it may lose its performance capacity. Other creditors have already taken preservation measures against Lanyue Energy's assets, including the goods under the bill of lading. Once the bill of lading is delivered to Lanyue Energy, CCB Liwan Sub-branch may lose its security interest in the bill of lading or the goods under the bill of lading. Under these circumstances, CCB Liwan Sub-branch's refusal to release the documents based on the right to suspend performance due to insecurity does not constitute a breach of contract, and certainly cannot serve as a reason to exempt or mitigate Lanyue Energy's payment liability under the letter of credit or the guarantee liabilities of Lanhai Shipping and Lan Wenbin. Therefore, this Court does not support the above claims of Lanyue Energy, Lanhai Shipping, and Lan Wenbin.

2. Regarding whether CCB Liwan Sub-branch has priority in satisfaction from the proceeds of disposing of the goods involved in the case.

In this case, CCB Liwan Sub-branch claims that it has a pledge of rights under the bill of lading. According to the provisions of Article 224 of the Property Law of the PRC regarding the establishment of a pledge of rights, establishing a pledge of rights under a bill of lading requires two concurrent conditions: first, both parties have signed a written contract for establishing a pledge of rights under the bill of lading; second, the requirement of publicity for property rights is met by delivering the document of title, i.e., the bill of lading, to the pledgee. CCB Liwan Sub-branch holds the bill of lading and thus satisfies the publicity requirement for establishing a pledge of rights under the bill of lading. Therefore, in determining whether it has a pledge of rights under the bill of lading, the key is whether there is a contractual basis. CCB Liwan Sub-branch claims that the Trust Receipt issued by Lanyue Energy to CCB Liwan Sub-branch has the nature of a pledge contract, but looking at the content of the Trust Receipt, Lanyue Energy intended to transfer ownership of the bill of lading and the goods under the bill of lading to CCB Liwan Sub-branch as security for the performance of its repayment obligations. Although the content of the Trust Receipt reflects the intention to secure CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim using the bill of lading and the goods under the bill of lading, that intention is to provide security by transferring ownership of the goods under the bill of lading, which is clearly different from a pledge of movable property or a pledge of rights, and should not be regarded as the contractual basis for establishing a pledge of rights under the bill of lading.

However, Article 9(2) of the Special Agreement on Opening Letters of Credit entered into between Lanyue Energy and CCB Liwan Sub-branch provides that once Lanyue Energy defaults or any of the circumstances specified in the Trade Financing Facility Agreement that may jeopardize CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim occurs, CCB Liwan Sub-branch is entitled to exercise one or more of the following rights, among which item 4 provides the right to "exercise security rights," and item 5 provides the right to "require Party A to increase the margin or provide other guarantees acceptable to Party B." Based on the following two reasons, it can be considered that the "security rights" under item 4 and the "other guarantees" under item 5 refer to different things: First, from the facts found in this case, the margin referred to in item 5 has already been paid by Lanyue Energy, and "other guarantees" refer to the joint and several liability guarantees provided by Yuedong Electric Power, Lanhai Shipping, and Lan Wenbin as agreed between the parties, and the pledge of Lan Wenbin's 6% equity interest in Lanyue Energy. Second, from the perspective of systematic interpretation of the contract, when a contract term is subject to two or more interpretations, an interpretation that renders some contract terms superfluous should not be adopted; rather, an interpretation that gives each contract term a certain meaning should be adopted. Therefore, it should be considered that the provisions of items 4 and 5 have different functions and legal significance. Where the "other guarantees" under item 5 are clearly specified, the "security rights" under item 4 should refer to security rights other than those specified in item 5. As to the nature of the "security rights" under item 4, considering the contract terms and the facts of the case, it can be considered that they refer to a pledge of rights under the bill of lading. The reasons are as follows: First, the basic mechanism and practice of documentary letters of credit is that the issuing bank holds the bill of lading, and the applicant pays for and takes delivery of the documents; if the applicant does not pay, the issuing bank does not release the documents. Thus, the purpose of the issuing bank holding the bill of lading is to secure the realization of its claim. As discussed above, the issuing bank does not own the goods under the bill of lading; if it is not recognized as having a security interest in the bill of lading or the goods under the bill of lading, this would completely deviate from the trade practice and basic mechanism of documentary letters of credit regarding payment against documents, and would completely deviate from the transaction purpose of both parties to the documentary credit of securing the issuing bank's claim with documents such as the bill of lading under the letter of credit. Second, Article 9(2) of the Special Agreement on Opening Letters of Credit also includes item 3, in addition to items 4 and 5 above, which provides that once Lanyue Energy defaults or any of the circumstances specified in the Trade Financing Facility Agreement that may jeopardize CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim occurs, CCB Liwan Sub-branch has the right to "dispose of the documents and/or goods under the letter of credit." This provision indicates that CCB Liwan Sub-branch has the right to dispose of the bill of lading and/or the goods under the bill of lading in its own discretion; disposal certainly includes establishing a pledge over the bill of lading. By virtue of this prior grant of the power of disposal, an expression of intent by CCB Liwan Sub-branch at a later time to establish a pledge over the bill of lading it holds fully complies with the provision of item 3. Of course, even if CCB Liwan Sub-branch subsequently expresses an intention to use ownership of the goods under the bill of lading to secure its claim, that would also comply with item 3, but using ownership of the goods to secure a claim violates the principle of numerus clausus of property rights. Where CCB Liwan Sub-branch simultaneously claims both the use of ownership of the goods under the bill of lading to secure its claim and a pledge of rights under the bill of lading, the claim that is more consistent with legal provisions should be supported, and the disposal referred to in that provision should be determined as establishing a pledge of rights under the bill of lading. In summary, CCB Liwan Sub-branch holds the bill of lading, and a bill of lading can be used to establish a pledge of rights. The relevant contracts contain both a general agreement to provide security and a clear agreement to dispose of the bill of lading at its own discretion. Pursuant to Article 125 of the Contract Law of the PRC concerning contract interpretation and Article 224 of the Property Law of the PRC concerning pledge of rights, it should be determined that CCB Liwan Sub-branch enjoys a pledge of rights under the bill of lading.

Because the bill of lading has the attribute of a document of title, CCB Liwan Sub-branch exercises the pledge of rights under the bill of lading in the same manner as exercising a pledge over movable property under the bill of lading, that is, it has priority in satisfaction from the proceeds of appraising the goods under the bill of lading, converting them into cash, or selling them by auction. According to the facts found by this Court, the goods under the bill of lading have been sealed up by another court, and that court has already taken enforcement measures based on an effective judgment. In this regard, although CCB Liwan Sub-branch has raised an objection as a third party, this does not affect this Court's continued trial of this case and its determination that CCB Liwan Sub-branch enjoys a pledge of rights under the bill of lading. CCB Liwan Sub-branch may, based on this judgment, request to participate in the distribution of proceeds from enforcement from the enforcing court. If its pledge of rights under the bill of lading conflicts with other creditors' possible rights such as a possessory lien or a pledge of movable property over the goods under the bill of lading, that can be resolved according to law in the enforcement distribution proceedings. The second-instance original judgment found that CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim for priority in satisfaction from the proceeds of disposing of the goods under the bill of lading was a pledge of movable property and dismissed this claim on the ground that the movable property had not been delivered. This is clearly an error in the application of law and should be corrected.

3. Regarding whether Yuedong Electric Power and Lanhai Shipping should additionally bear liquidated damages liability at the rate of 0.05% per day.

The maximum guarantee contracts entered into between Yuedong Electric Power and CCB Liwan Sub-branch, and between Lanhai Shipping and CCB Liwan Sub-branch, respectively, stipulate that the scope of guarantee includes all debts under the principal contract, including but not limited to all principal, interest (including compound interest and penalty interest), liquidated damages, compensation, other amounts payable by the debtor to CCB Liwan Sub-branch, and costs incurred in realizing the claim and security rights. The first-instance original judgment combined interest and late payment liquidated damages and calculated them at 0.05% per day, to which all parties did not object. This can be used as the basis for this Court's analysis of the calculation standard for liquidated damages within the scope of the guarantee. The calculation standard of 0.05% per day for interest and late payment liquidated damages is equivalent to an annual rate of 18.25%. Over the past decade, for RMB loans from financial institutions, the highest interest rate for terms over five years was only 7.83%. Even using that highest annual rate to calculate the actual interest loss of CCB Liwan Sub-branch, in the calculation standard of 0.05% per day for interest and late payment liquidated damages, the liquidated damages calculation standard is equivalent to an annual rate of 10.42% (18.25% - 7.83%), which undoubtedly far exceeds 30% of the actual interest loss. Where CCB Liwan Sub-branch neither claimed nor provided evidence to prove other losses beyond the interest loss from late payment, the late payment liquidated damages borne by the guarantors within the scope of the guarantee alone already exceed 30% of the actual loss. Under these circumstances, the maximum guarantee contracts also stipulate that the guarantors shall additionally bear late payment liquidated damages at 0.05% per day outside the scope of the guarantee. This clearly constitutes a situation where the agreed liquidated damages are excessively higher than the loss as provided in Article 114 of the Contract Law of the PRC. Pursuant to that Article and Article 29 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation (II) on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Contract Law of the PRC, a people's court may, based on the debtor's claim, reduce the liquidated damages as appropriate. In their first-instance defenses, Yuedong Electric Power, Lanhai Shipping, and Lan Wenbin all raised the defense that "the guarantee liability should be the liability within the scope of the guarantee agreed by the parties, and a guarantee liability exceeding the guarantor's guarantee has no legal basis." This defense is a fundamental denial of the guarantor's additional liability for liquidated damages. The second-instance original judgment, applying the principle that a greater includes a lesser, concluded that "it is deemed that a defense of excessive liquidated damages has been raised," which is not improper. On the basis of finding that the guarantors had raised a claim of excessive liquidated damages, the second-instance original judgment granted CCB Liwan Sub-branch's request for the guarantors to bear joint and several guarantee liability for the late payment liquidated damages of the principal debt, but dismissed its request for the guarantors to additionally bear late payment liquidated damages at 0.05% per day. This is an appropriate adjustment of the agreed liquidated damages and is not improper. This Court affirms this. Although the first-instance original judgment correctly dismissed this particular claim by CCB Liwan Sub-branch, it erroneously applied Article 113 of the Contract Law of the PRC, which is clearly an error in the application of law and should be corrected. Furthermore, CCB Liwan Sub-branch only requested that Lanhai Shipping and Yuedong Electric Power bear this liability, and did not make such a claim against Lan Wenbin. The original judgment listed Lan Wenbin together with Lanhai Shipping and Yuedong Electric Power in analyzing whether these three persons should bear this liability, which exceeded the scope of CCB Liwan Sub-branch's claim. However, since the original judgment did not impose this liability on Lan Wenbin, this Court, while correcting the error in the original judgment, also affirms the result.

In conclusion, the original judgment found the basic facts clearly, but there were errors in the application of law, and the result was partially improper and should be corrected. Pursuant to Article 224 of the Property Law of the PRC, and Items 2 of Paragraph 1 of Article 170 and Article 207 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, this Court hereby rules as follows:

1. Paragraph 4 of the main text of the Civil Judgment (2014) Yue Gao Fa Min Er Zhong Zi No. 45 of the Guangdong High People's Court and the Civil Judgment (2013) Sui Zhong Fa Jin Min Chu Zi No. 158 of the Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court, Guangdong Province, are hereby set aside;

2. The judgment of the Guangzhou Intermediate People's Court, Guangdong Province (2013) Sui Zhong Fa Jin Min Chu Zi No. 158, items 1, 2, and 3 of the main text of the civil judgment, is affirmed.

3. China Construction Bank Corporation, Guangzhou Liwan Branch, shall have a priority right to be compensated from the proceeds obtained from the disposal of the goods corresponding to the bills of lading under the letters of credit involved in this case.

4. The other claims of China Construction Bank Corporation, Guangzhou Liwan Branch, are dismissed.

The court acceptance fee of the first instance is 473,898 yuan, and the preservation fee is 5,000 yuan. Guangdong Lanyue Energy Development Co., Ltd., Huilai Yuedong Electric Power Fuel Co., Ltd., Guangdong Lanhai Shipping Co., Ltd., and Lan Wenbin shall jointly bear 400,000 yuan, and China Construction Bank Corporation, Guangzhou Liwan Branch, shall bear 78,898 yuan. The court acceptance fee of the second instance is 1,921.69 yuan.
